#5 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, plus what's new on its slate and a funding angle.

## Where the project stands

The project is a lab-level effort with three members: Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you. One honest caveat: I can see the membership and its current slate, but the project's confirmed state (goals, method, blockers, milestones) isn't visible to me in this conversation, so I can't say how far along the work is or what's blocking it. If the state was last confirmed more than thirty days ago, it may be out of date — worth a quick refresh in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers

All three entered the slate this week (2026-11-10 to 2026-11-13):

1. **#6 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The most directly on-topic item: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. If Plastic pathways involves particle tracking of debris, this is a ready-made method and codebase to build on or cite.

2. **#10 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026, Remote Sensing). Relevant as a remote-sensing detection method: a YOLO11-based framework (with Dynamic Snake Convolution and CBAM) that detects and segments low-contrast, curved features in satellite imagery, applied to a decade of MODIS data. The same pattern — automated detection of hard-to-see ocean features from space — transfers well to spotting plastic accumulations or debris plumes in satellite imagery.

3. **#11 — "Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array"** (Ryan-Keogh & Thomalla, 2026, Science Advances). Less directly about plastic, but useful context: it shows how autonomous profiling floats (biogeochemical-Argo) fill the subsurface gap that satellite remote sensing can't, with basin-scale trends in the Atlantic, Southern and Pacific Oceans. If your pathways work pairs in-situ observations with satellite data, this is a strong recent example of that integration and of the observing-system gaps it addresses.

(The other new items — #4 on Arctic phytoplankton, #5 on a Pacific forecast system, #7 a comment, and #9 on multi-object tracking — are further afield from debris pathways.)

## One funding opportunity

**#3 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, €50,000,000; deadline 2027-02-16, still open). It funds strengthening the GOOS through observation equipment, observing-system experiments, and network optimization, with explicit attention to biodiversity and under-observed regions. A Plastic pathways proposal framed around closing observing gaps for marine debris — e.g., integrating in-situ and satellite observations of pollution into the GOOS framework — fits its scope well, and the deadline gives you about three months to prepare.

A second option if the first feels like a stretch: **#8 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)** (deadline 2027-02-15), which accepts unsolicited proposals for instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science — a good fit if the project has a new sensor or tracking-technology component.

If you'd like, I can dig into the full text of #6 or #10, or check the fit of #3 against the project's confirmed state once it's up to date.

results.content:
#10 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

#11 [paper] Basin-scale changes in net primary production from the biogeochemical-Argo array.
Authors: Thomas James Ryan-Keogh, Sandy Thomalla
Venue: Science Advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeb0994
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Estimating basin-scale changes in marine net primary production (NPP) while overcoming the limitation of remote sensing, which is restricted to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Using data from the biogeochemical-Argo array of autonomous profiling floats to estimate basin-scale NPP change via the carbon-based production algorithm.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The biogeochemical-Argo array, covering the Atlantic, Southern, and Pacific Oceans.
Abstract:
Marine net primary production is expected to be affected by climate change. Although remote sensing offers broad spatial and temporal coverage, it is limited to surface observations and cannot capture subsurface variability. Autonomous profiling floats provide critical depth-resolved measurements that help bridge this gap. Here, we use data from the biogeochemical-Argo array to estimate basin-scale change in net primary production using the carbon-based production algorithm. We find statistically significant negative trends across the Atlantic and Southern Oceans and positive trends in the Pacific Ocean. These changes, if occurring in response to climate forcing, raise concern due to the key role of phytoplankton productivity in sustaining marine ecosystems. These trends typically agree in direction and magnitude with those from satellites. Our findings highlight the value of the biogeochemical-Argo array in detecting change in ocean productivity, demonstrating its potential for sustained monitoring. These results underscore the need for integrated observing systems to capture the full extent of changing marine productivity.

final_text:
Here's the comparison.

**The short version: #1 fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) better.**

**Why #1 fits**

The project's core problem is getting reliable, timely ocean forecasts to the people who manage the coast (#14). Grant #1 is about strengthening the Global Ocean Observing System — deploying observation equipment, running observing-system experiments, optimising sensor networks, and making sure data delivery is "fit-for-purpose" and reaches service users. That is the upstream of what your project does: better, more continuous observations are what make marine heatwave forecasts possible in the first place. The grant explicitly names Copernicus Marine Service and the need for "reliable services" as outcomes, which is the same end-user logic as handing forecasts to coastal managers. The €50M scale and the 2027-02-16 deadline also give you room to build a substantial proposal.

**Why #2 is a weaker fit**

Grant #2 is tightly scoped to the Antarctic and Southern Ocean: continental shelves, bottom-water formation, sea-ice and ice-shelf dynamics, and long-term (decadal-to-millennial) projections of that specific region. Your project is about near-term (days-to-weeks) marine heatwave forecasting in coastal waters, with machine-learning data assimilation, delivered to coastal managers. The geographic focus (Antarctic/Southern Ocean), the timescale (near/mid/long-term projections rather than operational forecasts), and the emphasis on cryosphere–ocean–ice interactions don't line up with what #3 is doing. The €5–11M amount and 2027-09-23 deadline are also less generous.

**The biggest doubt on #1**

#1 is a large, infrastructure-heavy call that leans on governance, network optimisation, and multi-stakeholder coordination with industry and public authorities. If the project's current work is mostly ML forecasting and data assimilation without a strong observing-network or governance component, you'd need to frame the proposal around how better observations enable the forecasts — which is a real but non-trivial bridge to build.

**What I could not check**

I don't have the project's confirmed goals, milestones, or budget from the system, so I'm comparing the grants against the lab's stated focus (#14) and the project's name and slate. If you can confirm the project's specific aims in the app, I can sharpen the fit assessment. I also can't see any eligibility rules (citizenship, institution type, consortium size) in either grant text, so those would need to be checked against the full call documents before you commit to either.

# Reviewing a project

1. `projects_get` for goals, confirmed state, blockers, milestones,
   developments in effect and members. Note when the state was last confirmed;
   past thirty days, say it may be out of date.
2. `projects_feed` for the current slate, in rank order, with when each item
   entered. "New this week" means it entered the slate this week.
3. Tie items to blockers: for each open blocker, which slate item (if any)
   speaks to it, and why. Cite both by #n.
4. End with what the team might do next, phrased as suggestions. You cannot
   change the project; point to the app for edits.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

It's squarely on your project's core question — ML MHW forecasts evaluated against persistence — and would anchor a methods/results paper for a data-analysis venue.

A 2026 particle-tracking/beaching result that fits the debris-pathways theme and would give your IGARSS submission a concrete, recent methodological hook.

One caveat: I've only read the abstracts and Mycelium's summaries of #31 and #39, not their full texts. If you want, I can check whether Mycelium holds the full text of either and pull the specific sections you'd cite.

#30 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#41 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Here's what I found.

## Best-fit open grant: #9 (GOOS)

Of the open grants on the Plastic pathways slate, **#9 "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System"** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16, still open) is the closest fit. The call asks for work that stabilises and operationalises the global ocean observing system — observation deployment, observing-system experiments, and network optimisation — and a marine-litter pathways project can frame its transport modelling and field validation as exactly that kind of observing-system work. The biggest doubt: the call's emphasis is on biodiversity and areas beyond national jurisdiction, so the proposal would need to lean hard on the *observation and data* side of the project rather than the policy side.

The other open grant on the slate, **#16 (NSF OTIC)**, is a weaker fit: it funds instrumentation development with broad applicability to ocean science, and no one in the lab has a declared profile covering instrumentation development. The other open grants I checked in the corpus (#19 harbours, #21 waterborne transport, #25 coastal resilience) are about ports, shipping fuels, and climate adaptation — none of them is about plastic pathways.

## Who should lead

- **You** — the nightly ranking named you for #9: your data-assimilation-with-ML work for ocean forecasting is read as strengthening the observing system's outputs (declared interest). As PI you'd be the natural lead.
- **Priya Raman (#4)** — also named for #9: her satellite ocean-colour remote sensing for water quality maps onto the call's "strengthened observing capacities and data coordination" (declared interest). She'd be the strongest co-lead or section owner for the remote-sensing component.
- **Jonah Whitcombe (#3)** — declared interests in marine litter and Lagrangian analysis make him the natural owner of the pathways-modelling core of the project.

Gaps no one in the lab covers: observing-system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimisation, and areas beyond national jurisdiction. The call also asks for industry partners — a role no one here is matched to.

## Partners outside the lab

I can't name specific people: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and I found no co-authorship path from you to Priya that runs only through people you can see. What I can say is what the call itself asks for, so you know what to look for when you build the consortium:

- **Observing-system experiment / OSSE expertise** — someone who has run OSEs or OSSEs (a gap in the lab)
- **Network optimisation** for observing networks
- **Areas beyond national jurisdiction** — a partner with ABNJ or GOOS governance experience
- **Industry / technology providers** — the call explicitly expects SMEs and maritime-industry partners for validation and deployment

If you'd like, I can search the corpus for papers or grants from groups that have done OSEs or OSSEs in ocean observing, to help you shortlist candidates.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Here's what I found across all three parts:

---

## Best-fitting open grant: #4 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System

Of the ten open grants on the project's slate, **#4** is the strongest fit for the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1). The call asks for proposals that stabilise and operationalise the global ocean observing system, with attention to climate resilience and reliable services — which maps directly onto the project's core work in ocean data assimilation and SST forecasting for marine heatwave early warning. The deadline is **16 February 2027**, and the amount is **€50 million**.

The next-best candidate is **#3** (NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination, deadline 15 Feb 2027), which is about instrumentation development with broad applicability. It's a looser fit: the project's ML data-assimilation work is more about analytical capability than new hardware, and no lab member's declared profile covers its core slot.

The remaining grants (#5 carbon, #6 Antarctica, #7 biodiversity remote sensing, #8–#9 geology/drilling, #10 blue forests, #11 wave energy, #12 tourism) are either off-topic or only tangentially related.

**Biggest doubt on #4:** the call emphasises areas beyond national jurisdiction, deep-sea and polar gaps, and biodiversity observations. The project's focus is on coastal/subseasonal SST forecasting, which is a narrower, more regional angle. You'd need to frame the heatwave early-warning work as a concrete service that the GOOS data infrastructure enables, and be ready to justify why a coastal forecasting use case belongs in a call that leans toward global-scale gaps.

---

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking and the slot-matching both point to **you (Mara Ellison)** as the natural lead:

- You cover the core slot — "stabilise, strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system" — with your declared work in **ocean data assimilation with ML**. That is the analytical engine the call is asking for.
- **Priya Raman (#16)** is the strongest co-lead or co-PI: her declared **satellite ocean remote sensing** work covers the same slot from the observation side, and the ranking names her first for profile fit.

**Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#18)** (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML) and **Sun-hee Park (#17)** (ocean data tools) round out the team well — Tomás brings the physics grounding for the forecasting models, Sun-hee the data-infrastructure angle the call values.

- Observing system experiments (OSEs) / simulation experiments (OSSEs)

- Industry partners (the call explicitly asks for them)

You'll want to recruit at least one partner with OSE/OSSE experience and one industry or service-operator partner (e.g., a Copernicus Marine Service operator or a marine-technology SME) to close those gaps.

---

## Who outside the lab could partner

Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I can't pull a list of external people who have consented to be matched. What I can say from what's visible:

- The call's own text names the communities it wants: **GOOS/IOC-UNESCO observing-network operators, Copernicus Marine Service, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, and maritime industries**. Those are the natural partner pools.
- The project's concept gaps — **sea surface temperature** and **fisheries** — are held by no current lab member's declared profile. A partner who brings SST reanalysis expertise (e.g., from a national meteorological or oceanographic service) or a fisheries-impact angle would close both gaps at once.
- For the OSE/OSSE and network-optimisation gaps, a partner from an established observing-systems group (e.g., a GOOS regional network or a Copernicus Marine Service centre) would be the most direct fit.

If you'd like, I can search the corpus for specific papers or groups working on OSEs/OSSEs for SST or heatwave forecasting to help you identify concrete external collaborators. Just say the word.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. The projects should contribute to a better understanding of the biophysical potential for marine mitigation approaches (in particular carbon dioxide removal) and their implications over relevant timeframes, including feedbacks. The analysis should also include responses to ambitious mitigation (e.g., atmospheric stabilisation in line with policy objectives). Projects should build on the results of related earlier projects, in particular those under call HORIZON-CL6-2022-CLIMATE-01-02.

#7 [grant] Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/295449
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 
Abstract:
The Marine Geology and Geophysics Core Program supports research on all aspects of the geology and geophysics of the present ocean basins and margins, as well as those of the Great Lakes.

The Program supports science that includes:

- Structure, composition, tectonics, and evolution of the oceanic lithosphere

- Paleoceanography, paleoclimate, and sea level change

- Submarine volcanology, petrology and geochemistry of the oceanic crust and upper mantle lithosphere

- Marine hydrogeology, water-rock interaction, seeps and gas hydrates

- Hydrothermal venting and in situ fluid processes, and associated geochemistry

- Geochemical indicators of life operating below the seafloor

- Marine sedimentology, stratigraphy, sediment transport, and diagenesis

- Mid-ocean ridge spreading, back-arc rifting, transform processes, and ocean island/seamount formation and evolution

- Submarine components of subduction zone systems and passive margins

- Marine geohazards (e.g., earthquakes, faulting, mass wasting, geological aspects of tsunamis)

- Coastal processes (e.g., geological aspects of hurricanes, sea-level change, erosion, offshore deposition)

The Marine Geology and Geophysics Program supports acquisition of new field data and the leveraging of and/or synthesis of existing data. The program supports analytical and laboratory experimental projects, methods development, and modeling. All activities should have relevance to and advance the understanding of marine geoscience processes. The Program interfaces with NSF programs across the Geosciences and across the Agency. For proposals that cross between Programs, proposers should contact the relevant Programs to seek guidance on submission.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Advancing basic research in the marine geosciences regarding climate, environmental, crustal, and observatory science objectives.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A multi-platform approach using a non-riser vessel for high-resolution cores, a heavy riser-equipped vessel for deep sedimentary and crustal layers, and mission-specific platforms for high-latitude and shallow-water projects.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) involving the JOIDES Resolution, Chikyu, and Mission Specific Platforms (MSP).
Abstract:
International Ocean Discovery Program Operations

The International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) serves to advance basic research in the marine geosciences and is supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and its international partners. The science plan, Illuminating Earth's Past, Present, and Future: The International Ocean Discovery Program Science Plan for 2013-2023, provides justification for the United States' participation in the IODP and reflects the top priorities of the international science community. A multi-platform approach is required to address the goals outlined in the IODP science plan, including a non-riser vessel to collect widely-distributed high-resolution cores to address climate, environmental, crustal and observatory science objectives; a heavy riser-equipped vessel to reach the deep sedimentary and crustal layers; and mission-specific platforms to support high-latitude and shallow-water projects.

The light drillship, JOIDES Resolution, is provided by the U.S. National Science Foundation. Science operations for the JOIDES Resolution are conducted through a Cooperative Agreement with Texas A&M University with scientific planning conducted by the JOIDES Resolution Facility Board.

The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) of Japan provides the heavy drillship, Chikyu (Earth), to conduct the deep drilling projects in the new program. The Center for Deep Earth Exploration of the Independent Administrative Institution, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) operates the vessel for IODP. Scientific planning for Chikyu IODP operations is conducted by the Chikyu IODP Board.

Mission Specific Platforms (MSP) are provided by the European Consortium for Ocean Research Drilling (ECORD). The ECORD Facility Board conducts scientific planning for MSP expeditions and the platforms themselves are operated by the European Science Operator (ESO).

A Science Support Office (SSO) is provided by Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego under a Cooperative Agreement with the National Science Foundation. The SSO’s primary tasks include:

- providing logistical support for the JOIDES Resolution Facility Board and its advisory panels

- overseeing the proposal submission and review process

- managing the Site Survey Data Bank

- providing a gateway website to IODP scientific planning

U.S. scientific community involvement in IODP is facilitated by the United States Science Support Program (USSSP) for Ocean Drilling. USSSP is run by Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia University under a Cooperative Agreement with the National Science Foundation. USSSP’s primary tasks are:

- support for U.S.-based researchers to participate on IODP expeditions, participate on the IODP advisory panels, and conduct initial post-expedition research

- support for planning and thematic workshops and pre-drilling activities to collect, refine, and/or integrate site specific and/or regional data that aid in planning drilling expeditions

- support outreach activities on IODP drilling platforms, for graduate students fellowships, and an IODP-themed lecture series.

Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration, and management of blue forest ecosystems (marine and coastal vegetated habitats) within European sea basins to meet EU climate, biodiversity, and restoration goals.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Innovative multidisciplinary projects integrating active and passive restoration, conservation efforts (e.g., managing Marine Protected Areas), innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., nature credits), multi-sensor research and monitoring, and community engagement, tailored to specific sea basins.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European sea basins, specifically one of four 'lighthouse' areas: Atlantic and Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North Sea, or Danube River basin (including Black Sea), involving EU Member States and Associated Countries.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Increased area and improved condition of marine and coastal vegetated habitats within EU waters through effective on-site conservation, restoration and management of activities to help deliver on the objectives of the Nature Restoration Regulation;

- Maintained and enhanced capacity of blue carbon ecosystems to naturally store carbon, supporting EU climate mitigation goals;

- Enhanced capacity of marine vegetated habitats/blue carbon ecosystems to support biodiversity and fisheries;

- Established novel financing and incentive mechanisms that support conservation, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems projects;

- Raised public awareness and improved community participation in blue forest ecosystems protection, restoration and management activities, ensuring long-term involvement.

Scope:

This topic seeks innovative multidisciplinary projects that will advance large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems, focusing on the assessment of ecological interactions, restoration of degraded ecosystems, conservation, and sustainable management within European sea basins. Projects are required to develop collaborations with EU Member States and Associated Countries national and regional agencies and authorities and policy makers and engage with local communities, researchers and NGOs. The direct involvement of relevant authorities and stakeholders in the consortium is strongly encouraged.

Proposals should target the development and implementation of comprehensive strategies that integrate blue carbon ecosystems into marine biodiversity frameworks, in particular in the implementation of the national restoration plans under the Nature Restoration Regulation.

Proposals are expected to show how their activities and results will help achieve the Mission’s objectives and targets. The basins / Mission “lighthouses” include the river basins flowing into the respective sea basins.

Amount: €380,000–€43,000,000

Deadline (application): 2027-03-31
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The development and demonstration of cost-effective wave and tidal energy systems that can survive in harsh ocean environments with minimal environmental impact, addressing the Strategic Energy Technology (SET) Plan’s research and innovation priorities.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A 5-year project structured into three challenges (Breakthrough, Validation, Demonstration) involving direct consortium activities and Financial Support to Third Parties (FSTP) calls. It includes the development of innovative devices, sustainable materials, mooring systems, AI-based condition monit…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European level, utilizing controlled environments such as test rigs, test tanks, semi-enclosed basins, or dedicated real-sea demonstration sites with instrumented monitoring infrastructure.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all following expected outcomes:

- Advance in the realisation of the Strategic Energy Technology (SET) Plan’s research and innovation priorities and targets for ocean energy;

- Energy producers and consumers benefit from increased performance of wave and tidal energy technologies with the focus on efficiency and flexibility, reduced cost, improved reliability and sustainability, operation and maintenance, robustness and security during all stages of the lifetime of an ocean energy farm from installation, operation and maintenance to decommissioning;

- Efficient and effective support to ocean energy research and innovation through alignment and cooperation among different actors, avoiding fragmentation of efforts providing effectively a significant developmental boost of wave and tidal energy technologies.

- Increased contribution of ocean energy to the energy system, with minimal impacts on health and the environment (notably biodiversity) and at the lowest possible cost.

Scope:

The action contributes to address the Strategic Energy Technology (SET) Plan’s research and innovation priorities[1] and targets[1] for ocean energy focussing on wave and tidal energy development. It will take into account the input defined in this context by the Implementation Working Group on ocean energy (IWG ocean), the European Technology and Innovation Platform on ocean energy (ETIP Ocean)[3] and the European Energy Research Alliance (EERA) joint programme on ocean energy[4].

The overarching objective is the development and demonstration of cost-effective wave and tidal energy systems that can survive in a harsh ocean or sea environment with minimal impacts on health and the environment and biodiversity. The challenge is open to proposals seeking to steer wave and tidal energy development for different type of resources in an effective way at a European level and to bring these technologies to the market. In this action the following can be considered:

- The development and demonstration in controlled environment of innovative wave energy devices.

- The development and demonstration in controlled environment of innovative next generation tidal energy devices

- The development and demonstration of new sustainable materials in ocean energy converters, moorings and foundations whilst ensuring structural integrity, durability and circularity can be considered.

- The development and demonstration of sustainable tailored mooring and connection of electrical or other power transmission systems (cable system, electrical equipment, ....) for wave and tidal energy devices. Advance combined mooring and electrical connectors or hydraulic power transmission to reduce component cost and number of connection operations, included in systems for sharing an anchor between devices in arrays. Develop novel systems for safe and quick connection/disconnection that do not require large vessels and/or diving teams.

- The instrumentation for condition monitoring and predictive maintenance of ocean energy devices and structures. Apply recent advances in condition and structural health monitoring from other sectors to ocean energy. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in ocean energy technology development.

- Advanced manufacturing of ocean energy devices and structures and auxiliary equipment considering reduced energy, manufacturing costs and materials consumption, high production throughput and optimization of logistics.

- Development of technologies and solutions for the installation, maintenance and decommissioning of wave and tidal energy devices.

The validation and demonstration of new ocean energy technologies should be done in a controlled environment meaning that this is done under monitored and reproducible conditions, using for instance, test rigs and test tanks, semi-enclosed basins, or dedicated real-sea demonstration sites with instrumented monitoring infrastructure.
